blocks.text: Few things are as closely tied to Turkmenistan as a horse. The Akhal-Teke is a breed from the oases at the foot of the Kopetdag mountains, on the southern edge of the Karakum desert. Its name joins the Akhal oasis and the Teke, the Turkmen tribe that bred it.

It is a long, slim horse with a long neck, a narrow chest and fine legs, built for speed and stamina rather than for pulling loads. Its short coat is so fine that many Akhal-Tekes shine with a metallic gleam. The effect is strongest on golden horses, which is why the breed is often called the golden horse.

Horses of this kind have a long history in the region. The Livestock Conservancy, an American organization that works for rare breeds, reports remains of tall, fine-boned horses from about 2400 BCE in southern Turkmenistan, and Encyclopaedia Britannica writes that the breed has served in cavalry and in races for some 3,000 years. Turkmen breeders kept their horses' pedigrees by memory and passed them on by word of mouth.

The breed's stamina became famous in 1935, when a group of riders took Akhal-Tekes from Ashgabat to Moscow, across the Karakum, in 84 days. Accounts of the distance vary; The Livestock Conservancy gives about 4,000 km.
Today the Akhal-Teke is rare: The Livestock Conservancy lists it as a threatened breed. In Turkmenistan it is a national symbol, and an Akhal-Teke stands at the centre of the state emblem.

In December 2023, UNESCO added the art of Akhal-Teke horse breeding and the traditions of horse decoration to its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The listing is about people as much as horses: how foals are named, cared for and trained, the beauty contests and races, and the decorated harness and jewellery that horses wear at weddings and festivals. These skills are passed on in families as well as at riding schools and colleges.

blocks.title: A word for a fine horse
blocks.text: The everyday word for a horse is *at*, with a short a: not the *at* with a long a that means **name**. For a fine riding horse, and the Akhal-Teke above all, Turkmen also uses *bedew*.
With the words of this unit, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Bu at sary. Ol at gara. Bu atlar owadan.
blocks.en: This horse is golden yellow. That horse is black. These horses are beautiful.

questions.q: In *Bu at sary*, what does *at* mean?
questions.explain: Here *at* has a short a and means **horse**. *at* with a long a means **name**.
